planting.note: Set out young plants or rooted softwood cuttings in spring in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; performs poorly where summer heat and humidity are extreme, so it suits Mountain West, high-plains, and Pacific Northwest xeriscapes better than the humid Gulf Coast.

directions: Set out young plants or rooted softwood cuttings in spring in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; sunrose forms a low, spreading, semi-evergreen mat of small gray-green leaves that disappears under a flush of single or double, saucer-shaped flowers in yellow, orange, pink, red, or white for several weeks in late spring and early summer. It is a classic choice for rock gardens, dry stone walls, and gravel edging in cooler, drier climates, but performs poorly where summer heat and humidity are extreme, so it suits Mountain West, high-plains, and Pacific Northwest xeriscapes better than the humid Gulf Coast. Shear lightly after the main bloom to encourage a tidier habit and occasional rebloom, and avoid rich soil or excess water, both of which shorten its lifespan.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; grown from semi-hardwood cuttings since seed propagation is not commercially practiced.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; shiny xylosma is grown chiefly for its glossy, bronze-red new growth maturing to lustrous bright green foliage rather than for its small, inconspicuous, fragrant greenish-yellow flowers, which are followed by black berries on female plants. It responds exceptionally well to shearing and is widely used as a formal or informal hedge, screen, espalier, or small patio tree in California, Texas, and Gulf Coast landscapes. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, poor soil, and urban conditions with ease, and the arching, somewhat thorny branches make it a useful barrier planting as well as an ornamental one.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade; typically propagated by semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade; red escallonia produces glossy, aromatic, dark green leaves and clusters of small, tubular, crimson-red flowers over a long summer bloom season that draws hummingbirds and bees. It is a mainstay hedge and screening shrub of coastal California and Pacific Northwest gardens because of its outstanding tolerance for salt spray, wind, and fog, though it prefers more consistent moisture than a true desert xeriscape plant. Shear or hand-prune after the main flush of bloom to keep an informal hedge dense, and site it where air circulates freely to minimize leaf spot in humid coastal conditions.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, ideally within sight or scent of the coast; strictly a warm coastal plant, suffering damage below the high 20s F.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, ideally within sight or scent of the coast; New Zealand Christmas tree is prized above all for its extreme tolerance of salt spray, wind, and sandy soil, thriving on exposed bluffs and beachfronts where few other flowering woody plants survive. Established plants are strikingly drought tolerant, drawing on deep roots once they are past their first year or two in the ground. Brilliant crimson, bottlebrush-like flower clusters cover the leathery, silver-backed leaves in a spectacular late-spring to early-summer display, and the plant can be maintained as a dense large shrub or screen with pruning, or allowed to develop into a picturesque small tree over many years. It is strictly a warm coastal plant, suffering damage below the high 20s F.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or small container plants in spring once the soil has warmed, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; roots readily from stem cuttings and is rarely propagated from seed in cultivation.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or small container plants in spring once the soil has warmed, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; coral creeper spreads by rooting stems as it grows, forming a low, dense mat useful as a border edging or filler beneath larger shrubs and trees. Salmon-pink to coral-red tubular flowers appear in flushes almost year-round in frost-free climates, attracting butterflies and hummingbirds, and the semi-glossy foliage stays attractive in light shade where many flowering groundcovers thin out. It is easy to propagate and quick to fill in a bed, but is strictly tropical and tender, dying back or dying out in any real frost.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or small container vines in spring after frost danger has passed, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun with a trellis, obelisk, or fence to twine on.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or small container vines in spring after frost danger has passed, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun with a trellis, obelisk, or fence to twine on. Firecracker vine is named for its small, tubular, two-toned red-and-yellow flowers that resemble tiny lit firecrackers and appear in a near-continuous flush from spring through fall. It is a modestly sized, well-mannered twining vine rather than a rampant grower, making it a good choice for containers, hanging baskets, or a small trellis on a porch or patio in warm climates. Where winters bring hard frost it is usually grown as a container plant brought indoors, or replanted annually.
